Title of Study: Pseudo-labeling of transfer learning convolutional neural network data for human facial emotion recognition
Research Objective(s): To increase the accuracy of facial emotion recognition on human face images by developing a pseudo-labeling method for transfer learning of a deep convolutional neural network, specifically to overcome dataset flaws like class imbalance, lack of data of a certain class, and insufficient data volume.
Educational Level Targeted: Not specified (Mentions "online learning" as an application domain)
E-Learning Platform / Setting: Not applicable (Algorithmic/model development paper)
Participant Type: Not applicable (Uses existing public image datasets)

Number of Classes / Labels: 7 basic emotion classes (Surprised, Fearful, Disgusted, Happy, Sad, Angry, Neutral)
Label Annotation Method: Crowdsourced / Expert (RAF-DB is annotated with basic and compound emotions by multiple annotators, though paper just says "labeled")
Data Collection Context: In-the-wild (RAF-DB collected from the internet with variations in age, gender, ethnicity, head pose, lighting, occlusion)
Class Imbalance Addressed?: Yes (method: Pseudo-labeling is explicitly used to overcome class imbalance by adding confident predictions of underrepresented classes back into the training set).
Data Augmentation Applied?: Yes (RandomFlip, RandomZoom, RandomRotation, RandomTranslation added as layers at the input of the neural network)
Specific Model / Variant: MobileNet V1 (Modified with 3 additional Conv2D layers, MaxPooling2D layers, and Dense layers)
Fine-tuning Strategy: Progressive unfreezing (Stage 1: Freeze convolutional layers, train new classification layers. Stage 2: Fine-tune the entire CNN model with a very low learning rate)
Learning Rate / Scheduler: Described as "very low training speed" for fine-tuning; exact value not stated
Regularisation Techniques: Dropout (implied from previous works/literature review), Data Augmentation (RandomFlip, RandomZoom, RandomRotation, RandomTranslation)
Real-Time Capability Claimed?: Partially (Authors mention MobileNet V1 is designed for mobile applications and requires low computational resources, but do not explicitly test or claim real-time latency for this specific pipeline).
Deployment Environment: Mobile platforms (implied by choice of MobileNet V1)
Detection Framework Used: Not specified
Teacher Dashboard / Feedback System?: No
Emotion / Affect Categories: 7 basic emotions (Surprised, Fearful, Disgusted, Happy, Sad, Angry, Neutral)
Precision / Recall / F1-Score: F1-Score is the primary metric used for evaluation. Per-class F1 scores reported.
Baseline / Benchmark Comparisons: Baseline is the CNN-FER model trained without pseudo-labeling vs. CNN(Retrain)-FER model trained with pseudo-labeled data
State-of-the-Art (SOTA) Comparison?: No (Compares only against their own baseline iterations)
Ablation Study Conducted?: Yes (Compared iterations of the pseudo-labeling method: 1st iteration, 2nd iteration (best result), 3rd iteration (performance deteriorated))
Best Result Achieved (Summary): Overall F1 accuracy increased from 76% to 78% on RAF-DB after the 2nd iteration of pseudo-labeling. Significant per-class F1 increases for minority emotions: Surprise (71% to 77%), Fearful (64% to 69%), Sad (72% to 76%), Angry (64% to 74%), Neutral (66% to 71%). Happy (majority class) decreased from 91% to 86%.
Bias Types Identified: Class imbalance bias (accuracy drop in majority class "Happy" when minority classes are boosted)
Bias Mitigation Methods: Pseudo-labeling (adding high-confidence predictions of underrepresented classes back to the training set to balance the learning)
Dataset Limitations: Popular datasets (DISFA, CelebA, AffectNet, RAF-DB) have fundamental flaws: lack of data of a certain class, class imbalance, subjectivity and ambiguity of labeling, insufficient volume of data for deep learning.
Model / Technical Limitations: Third iteration of pseudo-labeling caused performance deterioration. Boosting minority classes via pseudo-labeling caused a decrease in accuracy for the majority class (Happy dropped from 91% to 86%).
Real-Time / Deployment Limitations: None explicitly stated
Identified Research Gap: Deep learning CNNs for FER suffer from poor accuracy when trained on popular datasets because those datasets contain fundamental flaws such as class imbalance, lack of certain class data, subjectivity in labeling, and insufficient data volume. Standard data expansion methods can create additional imbalances or false patterns.
Proposed Future Work: The pseudo-labeling method can be recommended for expanding the volume of training sets for deep learning of CNNs to overcome dataset shortcomings like class imbalance and lack of data. (No specific future research directions are explicitly outlined by the authors at the end of the paper).
Clear Research Objective supporting text: The authors explicitly state the aim of the research: "to increase the accuracy of facial emotion recognition on the image of a human by developing a pseudo-labeling method for transfer learning of a deep neural network" to specifically overcome dataset flaws like class imbalance and insufficient data volume.
Appropriate Methodology supporting text: The use of a lightweight pre-trained CNN (MobileNet V1) with a structured transfer learning and fine-tuning approach is appropriate. Most importantly, the implementation of a teacher-student pseudo-labeling pipeline (where high-confidence predictions on unlabeled data are fed back into training) is a highly suitable and established semi-supervised methodology for addressing the stated problems of class imbalance and data scarcity.
Reproducibility supporting text: The architecture choice (MobileNet V1), the added layers (3 Conv2D, MaxPooling2D, Dense), the number of epochs (10), the pseudo-labeling threshold (probability > 0.99), and the dataset splits (12,271 training, 3,068 test) are clearly stated. However, the code/model weights are not released, and critical hyperparameters such as the optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and loss function are omitted, making exact replication difficult.
Dataset Adequately Described supporting: The dataset source (RAF-DB), total size, and the specific 7 emotion classes are identified. The paper also explicitly discusses the dataset's class imbalance and challenging in-the-wild conditions (lighting, occlusion, etc.). However, the exact demographic composition (age, gender, ethnicity breakdown) of the dataset subjects is not detailed, and the annotation methodology is only briefly referenced rather than fully described.
Appropriate Evaluation Metrics supportin: Given the explicitly acknowledged severe class imbalance in the RAF-DB dataset, the authors correctly selected the F1-measure (harmonic mean of Precision and Recall) as the primary evaluation metric instead of relying solely on standard accuracy. They also provided per-class F1 scores and confusion matrices, which is essential for demonstrating that the pseudo-labeling method actually improved minority class recognition at the expense of the majority class.
Comparison to Baselines / SOTA supportin: The study includes a strong internal ablation study, comparing the baseline model (without pseudo-labeling) against the model across three iterative steps of pseudo-labeling. However, there is no comparison against current State-of-the-Art (SOTA) methods or other existing pseudo-labeling/augmentation techniques on the RAF-DB dataset, nor is there any statistical significance testing.
XAI Sufficiently Evaluated supporting te: No Explainable AI (XAI) methods were implemented or evaluated in this study. The focus was strictly on predictive performance, dataset augmentation, and the iterative pseudo-labeling training process.
Limitations Explicitly Acknowledged supp: The authors explicitly acknowledge the fundamental limitations of popular FER datasets (class imbalance, lack of data, subjectivity of labeling). They also report a notable limitation of their method: the 3rd iteration of pseudo-labeling caused performance to deteriorate, and improving minority class accuracy came at the cost of decreasing majority class ("happy") accuracy. However, they do not discuss broader model failure modes or formal threats to validity.

Clear Research Objective supporting text: The authors explicitly state their objective to "propose a novel model named DT-EFER" that "combines deep neural networks with transfer learning theory" for "dynamic facial emotion recognition from online video," specifically focusing on the differences between key images (exemplars) rather than the images themselves to improve recognition.
Appropriate Methodology supporting text: The methodology is highly appropriate for the dynamic, online video scenario. Using GoogLeNet for feature extraction combined with an exemplar-based clustering model is sound. Crucially, the integration of Transfer Learning (via KL-distance between current and previous exemplar sets) directly addresses the challenge of recognizing emotions from short, subsequent video clips by leveraging reliable data from the initial clip.
Reproducibility supporting text: The mathematical formulations, algorithm pseudocode, parameter grid search bounds, and dataset preparation (video clip splits) are detailed extensively. However, the code is not released, the exact GoogLeNet weights/pre-training are not specified, and the primary results for Accuracy and RandIndex are presented only visually in bar charts (Figures 4-7) rather than exact numerical tables, making precise replication and comparison difficult.
Dataset Adequately Described supporting: The datasets (BAUM-1s and CK+) are identified, and the number of subjects, video clips, frame sizes, and emotion classes are reported. The pre-processing steps (cropping, PCA dimensionality reduction) and the exact methodology for splitting the video into source and drift clips are clearly described. However, the demographic details (age, gender, ethnicity) of the subjects are omitted.
Appropriate Evaluation Metrics supportin: The study uses Accuracy and RandIndex (RI), which are suitable for evaluating clustering/classification performance. Time consumption is also reported, which is vital for an online video processing claim. However, Precision, Recall, and F1-score are omitted, which could provide better insight into class-specific performance, especially in potentially imbalanced dynamic video scenarios. Furthermore, plotting results in charts instead of providing exact numbers lowers the rigor.
Comparison to Baselines / SOTA supportin: The proposed DT-EFER model is compared against four relevant baselines: two exemplar-based clustering models (EEM, AP), one transfer learning model (TSC), and one deep learning model (DSAE). The comparison includes both recognition accuracy/clustering quality and time consumption across two different datasets. No statistical significance testing is performed, however.
XAI Sufficiently Evaluated supporting te: While no formal XAI methods (like Grad-CAM or SHAP) are used, the inherent architecture of the DT-EFER model provides a form of explainability by design. It identifies "exemplars"—actual representative image samples from the video stream that act as cluster centers. The authors note this advantage: "we can directly get a typical image of each emotion from the video." However, no user study or formal qualitative evaluation is conducted to validate the usefulness of these exemplars to human users.

However, they do not discuss the limitation of relying on the first video clip being highly reliable (if the first clip is noisy, the transfer learning fails), nor do they discuss the lack of multi-modal or in-the-wild generalization as a current limitation (only as future work).

There are no reports of accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, or AUC-ROC for the emotion or distraction classifiers. The results section only discusses autonomous learning competency indices and web portal visit frequencies, which evaluate the e-learning platform's impact on student behavior, not the AI model's detection performance.
Comparison to Baselines / SOTA supportin: The proposed system is not benchmarked against any baseline or current state-of-the-art models. While the authors mention accuracy rates from prior works (e.g., 92.75% for engagement levels), they do not compare their own trained model's performance against these or any other benchmarks. No statistical significance testing is performed for the AI components.

Critical flaws—such as the Haar Cascade's sensitivity to lighting/occlusion, the lack of temporal modeling for video data, the disconnect between the FER-2013 dataset and real e-learning expressions, and the fact that the system was never deployed in a real classroom—are completely omitted from the text.

Title of Study: A Facial Expressions Recognition Method Using Residual Network Architecture for Online Learning Evaluation
Source / Venue: Journal of Advanced Computational Intelligence and Intelligent Informatics (JACIII)
Research Objective(s): To propose a CNN-based model using a residual network architecture (FERES) for facial expression recognition, utilize image augmentation to improve results, and design an integrated system for LMS to evaluate online learning processes.
E-Learning Platform / Setting: Custom integration with a Learning Management System (LMS)
Sample Size (N): CK+ (927 images), Oulu-CASIA (1,440 images), JAFFE (213 images), FERS21 (599 images from 20 learners)
Gender Distribution: JAFFE (10 females); FERS21 (Males and females, exact % NR); Others: Not specified
Dataset Name(s): CK+, Oulu-CASIA, JAFFE, FERS21 (Custom)
Number of Classes / Labels: CK+, Oulu-CASIA, JAFFE (6 basic emotions + Neutral/Contempt variants); FERS21 (2 labels: Happiness, NO-Happy)
Label Annotation Method: Not stated
Data Collection Context: Lab-controlled (CK+, JAFFE, Oulu-CASIA) / In-the-wild (FERS21 - "collected from learners under fairly free conditions")
Class Imbalance Addressed?: Not stated (Paper notes FERS21 is imbalanced: 499 NO-Happy vs 100 Happiness, but no algorithmic mitigation like SMOTE is applied)
Data Augmentation Applied?: Yes (Gaussian noise, rotation, zoom, shift, horizontal flip. 11x enlargement for small datasets)
Specific Model / Variant: FERES (Custom ResNet model with 16 Residual Units divided into 4 blocks; 49 convolutional layers total)
XAI Evaluation Method: Qualitative visualisation (Observation that heatmaps focus on mouth and eye areas)
Real-Time Capability Claimed?: Yes ("captures face pictures... for every certain period of time... repeated at a predefined time period (I) until the learner stops")
Deployment Environment: Not specified (Server-side receiving images from LMS)
Detection Framework Used: MTCNN (Used for face detection preprocessing)
Teacher Dashboard / Feedback System?: Yes (Recognized results sent to LMS for recording and tracking learning activities; institutions use evaluation to improve teaching)
Emotion / Affect Categories: 7 basic (Ekman) + Neutral variations for public datasets; 2 custom (Happiness, NO-Happy) for FERS21
Baseline / Benchmark Comparisons: Yes (Compared against 7 other methods: Multi-task CNN, Attentional CNN, Dynamic Multi-task CNN, 2-channel CNN, etc.)
Ablation Study Conducted?: No
Best Result Achieved (Summary): 99.68% accuracy on the CK+ dataset; 95.33% on the real-world FERS21 dataset.
Dataset Limitations: Small N (JAFFE has very few images causing unstable validation; CK+ images are homogeneous); Lab-controlled only (CK+, Oulu-CASIA lack real-world pose/illumination variety); Class imbalance (FERS21 is heavily imbalanced towards NO-Happy).
Model / Technical Limitations: High computational cost (23.5 million parameters, described as "moderate size" but significantly larger than his later 2022/2023 works); Generalisation failure (FERS21 accuracy is notably lower than controlled datasets due to free conditions/varied poses).
Explainability Limitations: XAI not validated (Grad-CAM is only visually interpreted).
Real-Time / Deployment Limitations: Latency too high / Not tested in real classroom (Inference speed/FPS not reported; System is a proposed design, not a live deployment test).
Identified Research Gap: Existing FER models struggle with the diversity of people showing the same facial expressions, and state-of-the-art architectures often have massive computational complexity (hundreds of millions of parameters) that hinders practical integration into resource-constrained LMS systems.
Proposed Future Work: Improve accuracy and efficiency by applying state-of-the-art loss functions (beyond softmax) and advanced CONV blocks like "squeeze-and-excitation" (SE); Design an automatic image data collection system to build larger datasets for real-world application; Build a full monitoring/assistant application for online learning students.
Clear Research Objective supporting text: The paper explicitly states its aim to "propose a CNN-based model using a residual network architecture for FER problems... augment images to create a diversity of training data... [and] propose an integrated system for learning management systems to identify students and evaluate online learning processes."
Appropriate Methodology supporting text: The methodology is sound. The author designs a custom ResNet-based architecture (FERES), utilizes appropriate data augmentation strategies, and evaluates the model using a standard 10-fold cross-validation scenario across four different datasets (three public, one custom).
Reproducibility supporting text: The model architecture (block sizes, RU structure) and training parameters (lr=0.001, batch=64, epochs=200, Adam optimizer, augmentation ranges) are detailed. However, the code, model weights, and the custom FERS21 dataset are not publicly released, making exact replication impossible.
Dataset Adequately Described supporting: The paper provides a thorough description of the datasets. It lists the number of images, subjects, class labels, image format, and collection context. It explicitly details the class distribution for all datasets in Table 1, acknowledging the severe imbalance in FERS21.
Appropriate Evaluation Metrics supportin: Accuracy is reported across the 10-fold cross-validation, and confusion matrices are thoughtfully provided and analyzed for the public datasets. However, because the author explicitly acknowledges that the FERS21 dataset has a highly imbalanced distribution (499 vs 100), relying solely on accuracy is misleading; precision, recall, or F1-score should have been reported for FERS21.
Comparison to Baselines / SOTA supportin: The proposed FERES model is compared against seven other recent CNN-based methods from the literature across the CK+, Oulu-CASIA, and JAFFE datasets, demonstrating superior performance in most cases.
XAI Sufficiently Evaluated supporting te: Grad-CAM is used to generate heatmaps, and the author qualitatively observes that the model focuses on the mouth and eyes. However, there is no quantitative evaluation of the explanation quality (e.g., faithfulness metrics, robustness tests, or user studies), making the XAI evaluation purely descriptive.
Limitations Explicitly Acknowledged supp: The author acknowledges computational limitations ("owing to computing limitations, we only apply a small training time"), the small size of JAFFE causing unstable validation, and the lower accuracy on FERS21 due to free conditions. However, they do not explicitly discuss the limitations of evaluating a "real-world" LMS monitoring system almost entirely on lab-controlled, posed datasets (CK+, JAFFE, OuluCASIA), nor the risk of bias in the imbalanced FERS21 dataset.

Title of Study: YOLOv5 based student engagement and emotional states detection in e-classes
Source / Venue: Journal of Robotics, Networking and Artificial Life
Research Objective(s): To develop a novel approach (SER-YOLO) for early detection of cyberbullying by analyzing student engagement and emotional states in real-time within e-learning environments, using an enhanced YOLOv5 model.
Country / Geographic Context: Malaysia / China (Authors affiliated with UCSI University Malaysia and Yuncheng University China; Survey conducted in higher vocational colleges/universities).
Educational Level Targeted: Higher Ed (Higher vocational colleges and universities)
E-Learning Platform / Setting: Virtual classroom / E-class (Online learning environment)
Sample Size (N): 520 survey respondents (287 male, 233 female); 668 images in custom dataset; 11,000 images in refined FER2013 dataset.
Gender Distribution: Survey: 55.2% Male, 44.8% Female. (Dataset gender distribution not reported).
Dataset Name(s): FER2013, Custom (Self-constructed student facial expression dataset)
Modality/ies in Dataset: Static image (Frames extracted from classroom videos + public dataset images)
Number of Classes / Labels: 7 basic emotions (Anger, Surprise, Disgust, Happiness, Fear, Sadness, Neutral) mapped to engagement states (Mastery, Confusion, Non-mastery).
Label Annotation Method: Custom (Extracted frames from recorded sessions and labeled; FER2013 cleansed/filtered by authors)
Data Collection Context: Lab-controlled / Online lecture capture (Classroom videos surveilled)
Class Imbalance Addressed?: Yes (Method: Focal Loss incorporated to mitigate class imbalance)
Data Augmentation Applied?: Not stated (Standard YOLO augmentations like mosaic may be used by default, but not explicitly detailed in the text)
Primary DL Architecture: CNN / YOLO (One-stage object detector adapted for classification/detection)
Specific Model / Variant: SER-YOLO (Based on YOLOv5s-6.0)
Attention Mechanism Used?: Yes (Coordinate Attention [CA] module integrated into the backbone to strengthen channel characteristics and capture precise spatial data)
Fine-tuning Strategy: Full fine-tuning (Implied by training the enhanced network on the new datasets)
Loss Function(s): Custom (EIOU Loss for bounding box regression + Focal Loss for classification/sample imbalance)
Real-Time Capability Claimed?: Yes (Explicitly stated goal for real-time detection; YOLOv5 noted for reaching up to 140 FPS)
Inference Speed / Latency Reported?: No (While the text mentions YOLOv5 can reach 140 FPS, no specific inference speed/FPS is reported for the proposed SER-YOLO model on their hardware).
Deployment Environment: Edge device / Standard PC (Tested on Windows 10, Intel i5-11400H, NVIDIA RTX 3050)
Detection Framework Used: YOLOv5s-6.0
Teacher Dashboard / Feedback System?: Proposed only (Implied that it assists teachers in understanding learning experiences, but no system implemented).
Emotion / Affect Categories: 7 basic (Ekman) + 3 engagement states (Mastery, Confusion, Non-mastery)
Precision / Recall / F1-Score: Yes (Precision [P] reported. Self-constructed dataset overall: 87.3%; FER2013 overall: 75.6%)
Baseline / Benchmark Comparisons: Yes (Compared against the baseline YOLOv5 model)
State-of-the-Art (SOTA) Comparison?: Partially (Only compared against its own baseline, not other SOTA FER architectures like ResNet, VGG, etc.)
Ablation Study Conducted?: Partially (The paper describes enhancements—Soft NMS, CA module, EIOU+Focal Loss—but the results table only compares baseline YOLOv5 to the final SER-YOLO, without isolating the contribution of each individual component).
Cross-Dataset Validation?: Yes (Tested on both a self-constructed dataset and FER2013)
Best Result Achieved (Summary): On the self-constructed dataset, SER-YOLO achieved 87.3% Precision and 88.9% mAP@0.5 (an improvement of 3.9% in P and 3.0% in mAP@0.5 over baseline YOLOv5).
Bias Mitigation Methods: Not stated (Though Focal Loss addresses class imbalance, demographic bias is not discussed)
Dataset Limitations: Limited modalities (only facial expressions currently used).
Model / Technical Limitations: Not explicitly discussed in detail, though the lower performance on the FER2013 dataset (75.6% P) suggests difficulty with more varied/in-the-wild data compared to the controlled self-constructed dataset.
Real-Time / Deployment Limitations: Inference latency was not empirically validated/reported for the modified model, leaving real-time claims unproven in the experimental results.
Identified Research Gap: Existing real-time detection capabilities for student facial expressions are inadequate, and there is a lack of timeliness in identifying emotional states and cyberbullying incidents in complex e-learning settings.
Proposed Future Work: Broaden the scope to encompass not only facial expressions but also body postures and gestures to provide a more comprehensive understanding of classroom dynamics and strengthen cyberbullying prevention.
Clear Research Objective supporting text: The abstract clearly states: "This study introduces a novel approach for early detection of cyberbullying by analyzing student engagement and emotional states in real time. Our SER-YOLO model fuses an advanced YOLOv5... enriched by sophisticated methodological improvements."
Appropriate Methodology supporting text: The use of a YOLO variant is appropriate for the stated goal of real-time detection. The specific enhancements (Soft NMS for subtle expressions, CA mechanism for distant/multi-student scenarios, EIOU+Focal Loss for bounding box and class imbalance) logically address known challenges in classroom FER.
Reproducibility supporting text: The authors provide the exact hyperparameters (resolution 640x640, Adam optimizer, lr0=0.01, lrf=0.1, weight_decay=0.0005, epochs=300, batch_size=16), hardware specs, and software versions (PyTorch 1.8, Python 3.8). However, the self-constructed dataset is proprietary/not linked, and the exact configuration of the CA module integration is only briefly shown in a diagram without code repository provision.
Dataset Adequately Described supporting: The source of data (FER2013 + self-constructed) is stated, the cleaning process for FER2013 is mentioned, and the total image counts are given (11,000 and 668). However, the demographic makeup of the students in the self-constructed dataset is missing, and the 7-emotion class distribution within the datasets is not reported, making it hard to assess the severity of the class imbalance they tried to fix with Focal Loss.
Appropriate Evaluation Metrics supportin: The study uses Precision and mAP@0.5, which are standard for object detection models like YOLO. However, for facial expression recognition classification tasks, metrics like Accuracy, F1-score, or per-class Recall are typically expected and largely missing here (only overall Precision is emphasized).
Comparison to Baselines / SOTA supportin: The model is compared against the baseline YOLOv5, demonstrating the value of their enhancements. However, it is not compared against any other State-of-the-Art FER models or classification architectures (e.g., ResNet, VGG, or other attention-based CNNs), limiting the ability to benchmark this approach against the broader field.
XAI Sufficiently Evaluated supporting te: No Explainable AI methods were implemented or evaluated in this study.
Limitations Explicitly Acknowledged supp: The conclusion implicitly acknowledges a scope limitation by stating future work will broaden beyond facial expressions to body postures. However, they do not explicitly discuss the methodological limitations of their current model (e.g., the significant performance drop when tested on the FER2013 dataset compared to their custom dataset, or the unverified real-time inference speed of their modified architecture).

Limitations Explicitly Acknowledged supp: The authors do not explicitly discuss the limitations of their study. To solve the issue of missing intensity annotations, they use linear interpolation and Gaussian distributions. To solve identity bias in expressions, they use a Siamese-like CNN with neutral frame pairing. The approach is logically sound for joint FER and intensity estimation.

Dataset Adequately Described supporting: Public datasets are adequately referenced with sequence counts. The custom Child Empathy dataset is described (60 sequences, 1200 frames each, 30 TD / 30 ASD, emotional stimulus video described). However, demographic diversity, exact ages, and gender distributions are entirely missing.
Appropriate Evaluation Metrics supportin: For intensity estimation, they appropriately use PCC, ICC, and MAE. For expression recognition, they use accuracy. They break down accuracy into weak, combined, and peak expressions, which is highly appropriate given their focus on intensity-variant recognition.
Comparison to Baselines / SOTA supportin: The study extensively compares the proposed method against baseline VGG-16, traditional machine learning methods (CSPL, AdaGabor), and deep learning SOTA (PPDN, 3DCNN-DAP, DTAGN). They also conduct a thorough ablation study. However, no statistical significance testing (e.g., p-values) is reported.
XAI Sufficiently Evaluated supporting te: No Explainable AI (XAI) methods were implemented or evaluated in this study.
Limitations Explicitly Acknowledged supp: In the Conclusion, the authors explicitly state: "The present study is limited to constrained condition. As reported in the empathy analysis experiment, when head pose deviation or partial occlusion occurs, the proposed method fails to provide an accurate prediction for expression category and intensity." They also propose clear future directions to solve these specific limitations.

Clear Research Objective supporting text: The authors explicitly state their focus on "a step-by-step process of design and implementation of an adaptive E-learning system" with the main objective of "identification of features, the fusion of basic features to categorize the learner’s mood by taking the input as a video stream of participants" into four categories: active learner, passive learner, non-learner, and evaluative learner.
Appropriate Methodology supporting text: Using a CNN for facial emotion recognition from video frames is a standard and appropriate deep learning approach. Additionally, the rule-based mapping of recognized emotions to learner categories addresses the application goal. However, claiming a 97.40% accuracy on the FER2013 dataset is highly unusual and contradicts the general consensus in the literature (where FER2013 is a challenging, noisy dataset and SOTA typically ranges in the high 80s to low 90s for 7-class classification). This casts doubt on the methodological rigor, likely indicating overfitting, data leakage, or issues with the train/test split that were not addressed.
Reproducibility supporting text: The custom 13-layer CNN architecture is described layer-by-layer, and key hyperparameters are provided (Adam optimizer, lr=0.0001, batch size=64, 200 epochs). A confusion matrix for the 7-class problem is also notably absent.

However, the comparison lacks context, as the baseline accuracies reported for the same dataset are vastly lower (61% - 91%) than the proposed model's 97.40%, yet no analysis is provided for why their simple 13-layer CNN massively outperforms established deep architectures like VGGNet. No statistical significance testing is performed.

Appropriate Methodology supporting text: The methodology directly targets the research gap of heavy computation and privacy risks. Modifying MobileViT's fusion block reduces parameters, and using Knowledge Distillation (VOLO-D2 as teacher) recovers lost accuracy. The on-device processing framework logically solves the stated privacy concerns.
Reproducibility supporting text: The paper provides exceptional detail: specific hardware (i9-9900K, RTX 3090), software (Python 3.9, PyTorch 2.0, CUDA 11.3), dataset splits (8:1:1), and precise hyperparameters (lr=1e-4, cosine annealing, batch=16, 100 epochs, τ=7.0/9.0, λ=0.7). Appropriate Evaluation Metrics supportin: The study uses the F1-score (referred to as F-score) as the primary evaluation metric, which is highly appropriate for multi-class classification, especially when dealing with potentially unbalanced data, as it combines precision and recall. The inclusion of confusion matrices for the different sensor combinations further supports the robustness of the evaluation.
Comparison to Baselines / SOTA supportin: The study includes a strong internal ablation study comparing different sensor combinations (C1-C4) and compares the proposed IoT protocols (TS-MAC, R-MAC) against state-of-the-art legacy protocols (LLDN, LLDN-SS) for latency and reliability. However, there is no comparison of the proposed LSTM model's performance (95.1% F1) against other existing state-of-the-art deep learning models (e.g., CNNs, Transformers) applied to the same physiological dataset, nor is statistical significance testing reported.
XAI Sufficiently Evaluated supporting te: No Explainable AI (XAI) methods were implemented or evaluated in this study. The LSTM model acts as a black box to classify emotions, and there is no analysis of which physiological features or temporal segments the model is using to make its decisions.
Limitations Explicitly Acknowledged supp: The authors explicitly discuss several limitations regarding the practical deployment of their system. They note that using a large number of sensors (C4) is "often impractical," specifically highlighting that EMG sensors on the face/upper back and the RSP sensor under the armpit are impractical for real-life wearability. They also acknowledge that the R-MAC IoT protocol "sacrifices the data precision to achieve high reliability and low latency," which could cause limitations in other applications.

Clear Research Objective supporting text: The study explicitly aims to propose a novel student engagement prediction model for online learners based on facial emotion, encompassing four phases: preprocessing, feature extraction, emotion recognition via a hybrid IDBN+CNN, and engagement detection via improved entropy.
Appropriate Methodology supporting text: While combining feature extraction (AAM, SLBT, GBP, ResNet) and a hybrid classifier (IDBN+CNN) is a valid approach, the methodology feels highly engineered and somewhat disjointed. Feeding handcrafted features (like GBP and AAM) alongside deep features (ResNet) into a DBN+CNN is computationally complex, and the justification for this specific combination over end-to-end deep learning is weak. Additionally, mapping 7 basic emotions to binary engagement via a mathematical entropy threshold lacks empirical pedagogical validation.
Reproducibility supporting text: The mathematical formulas for feature extraction, model parameters (epochs, batch size, learning rates, dropout), and dataset sources are provided. However, the code is not released, the logic for the "improved entropy" engagement scoring is convoluted, and the dataset sizes reported for FER-2013 (1400 images) contradict the standard public dataset size (~35k), making exact reproduction questionable.
Dataset Adequately Described supporting: The names of the datasets (CK+, FER-2013) and the train/test splits based on learning percentages are provided. However, the description of FER-2013 is factually incorrect/inconsistent (states only 1400 photos instead of ~35,887), and no demographic details, class distributions, or annotation methods are discussed.
Appropriate Evaluation Metrics supportin: The study uses a comprehensive set of standard classification metrics: Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, Precision, F-measure, NPV, FPR, FNR, and MCC, evaluating the model thoroughly from multiple statistical angles.
Comparison to Baselines / SOTA supportin: The proposed hybrid model is compared against nine different baseline models (CNN, DBN, SVM, LSTM, RF, DCNN, BiLSTM, etc.) and performs ablation studies comparing the impact of its specific feature extractors and DBN components.
XAI Sufficiently Evaluated supporting te: No XAI methods were implemented or evaluated. The model acts as a black box, mapping facial features to engagement scores via a complex entropy formula without explaining which facial features or sequences drive the classification.
Limitations Explicitly Acknowledged supp: The authors mention general computer vision challenges (dynamic features, poor image quality, small face size in high-res images, visual background intricacies) in the literature review/objectives. However, they do not discuss the limitations of their own proposed model, its high computational complexity, the lack of real-world online learning validation, or the validity of their entropy-threshold mapping.

Appropriate Methodology supporting text: Modifying a proven CNN architecture (ResNet-50) with an attention mechanism (CBAM) and improved downsampling techniques to preserve spatial correlations is a highly appropriate and standard deep learning methodology for addressing FER feature extraction challenges and improving accuracy.

Clear Research Objective supporting text: The study explicitly aims to present an innovative approach to FER using a homogeneous ensemble CNN (HoE-CNN) to improve classification on imbalanced/multi-class datasets and transfer this model for future online learning applications.
Appropriate Methodology supporting text: Using a homogeneous ensemble of well-established CNN architectures is a sound and appropriate methodology to address the stated problems of class imbalance and the limitations of single models struggling with complex multi-class data.
Reproducibility supporting text: The dataset is public, and detailed hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, optimizer, epochs) are provided for each individual model in the ensemble. However, the specific code/weights are not released, the exact ensemble aggregation logic (Equation 1) is slightly ambiguously formatted in the text, and the base model pre-training details are assumed but not explicitly documented.
Dataset Adequately Described supporting: The dataset (FER2013), size (35,887), data splits, image resolution (48x48), class labels, and class imbalance (with specific distribution charts) are thoroughly described. The paper even notes the inherent noise/limitation of the dataset (~65% annotation accuracy).
Appropriate Evaluation Metrics supportin: Accuracy is reported and a confusion matrix is provided. However, for a dataset with severe class imbalance (which the authors identify as a key challenge), relying primarily on overall accuracy is insufficient. Precision, Recall, and F1-score (which are mentioned in the method section) are not explicitly reported as aggregate numerical values in the results section.
Comparison to Baselines / SOTA supportin: The proposed ensemble is thoroughly compared against its individual constituent models (ablation) and compared against four recent SOTA methods on the FER2013 dataset.
XAI Sufficiently Evaluated supporting te: XAI is not implemented or evaluated. The authors correctly identify in their discussion that ensemble methods sacrifice interpretability and that this is a challenge, but no XAI techniques (e.g., Grad-CAM, SHAP) were applied to the models to address this.
Limitations Explicitly Acknowledged supp: The authors openly discuss several limitations: the low annotation accuracy and class imbalance of the dataset, the poor performance on specific emotions (fear, sad, angry), the lack of interpretability of the ensemble, the computational scalability issues, and the practical deployment challenges (camera limitations, non-face detection) in real online learning environments.
